name: Identify major constellations
blurb: Twenty constellations is enough to orient yourself anywhere in your hemisphere and to never look at the night sky the same way again.
gear: A star chart or a planisphere
A red torch to preserve night vision
A stargazing app for checking yourself
steps: Start with the anchor: the Plough or the Southern Cross, depending on hemisphere, and learn to find it in any orientation.
Use star hopping: the Plough’s pointer stars find Polaris; its handle arcs to Arcturus and speeds on to Spica.
Learn the seasonal set for right now — Orion in winter, the Summer Triangle in summer — rather than all of them at once.
Learn five new constellations a week and revisit the old ones every session.
Learn to distinguish planets from stars: planets do not twinkle and stay near the ecliptic.
Go out on the same clear night each week and name everything you can before checking the app.
tips: Give your eyes 20 minutes to dark-adapt, and use a red torch so you do not lose it.
Constellations rotate through the night and the seasons. Learn the shapes relative to each other, not to the horizon.
Light pollution hides most of the sky. One trip somewhere dark is worth ten from a city.
proof: You name 20 constellations on a clear night, unaided, and use them to find north or south.
